subject: Discovery recap: Finly - p95 latency & streaming UX / next steps
messages:
From: Marissa Cole <marissa@redwood.ai>
To: Alex Johnson <alex@finly.com>
Cc: Aditya Rao <aditya_rao@redwood.ai>, Ethan Park <ethan_park@redwood.ai>
Date: Sat, 28 Nov 2026 19:10:00 +0000
Subject: Discovery recap: Finly - p95 latency & streaming UX / next steps

Alex - thanks for the time today. Quick recap from our call so we have alignment and clear next steps. Feel free to correct anything I missed.

Pain points (what keeps you up at night)
- p95 generation latency is inconsistent: currently seeing ~600-900ms for short prompts, spikes up to 1.5s under load.
- Streaming UX feels choppy for long responses; customers expect token-by-token playback with low startup time.
- Concurrency problems during peak batch jobs and nightly reports - backend starts queuing and tail latency spikes.

Current stack
- Frontend: React app using a Node.js backend (server-side requests to LLM).
- LLM calls: currently using OpenAI API for generation + Redis for short-term caching.
- Hosting: AWS (us-east-1) with a mix of g4dn and some CPU fallback nodes.

Success criteria (what would make this a win)
- p95 token-complete latency <= 200ms for typical 256-token responses.
- Streaming startup (first bytes) <= 150ms and steady token throughput for the rest of the stream.
- Sustained concurrency of 100-150 concurrent requests with p95 <= 300ms.
- No functional regressions; output quality maintained (same prompts/evals pass).

Immediate asks / next steps
1) I attached a short analysis template (redwood-p95-analysis-template.xlsx) - if you can drop in a couple of representative traces / sample request/response sizes, we can do an initial estimate.
2) Please share a short network trace or an example slow request (we discussed you sending a trace).
3) We'll spin up a short technical session with Aditya and Ethan to dig into concurrency/streaming implementation (30-45m).
4) Propose a 2-week PoC: baseline measurements + targeted optimizations (caching + streaming tuning) - we can scope after the technical session.

Proposed timeline
- Technical deep-dive: next week (Nov 30-Dec 2) - Marissa/Aditya/Ethan
- PoC kickoff: week of Dec 7 (2 weeks)

If that all looks right I'll schedule the deep-dive and share a short Mutual Action Plan. Thanks again - excited to see if we can get Finly to sub-200ms p95 for your main flows.

Best,
Marissa Cole
Account Executive, Redwood Inference
marissa@redwood.ai
+1 (415) 555-0123

Attachments: redwood-p95-analysis-template.xlsx

From: Alex Johnson <alex@finly.com>
To: Marissa Cole <marissa@redwood.ai>
Cc: Chris Mayer <chris@finly.com>
Date: Sat, 28 Nov 2026 20:02:00 +0000
Subject: Re: Discovery recap: Finly - p95 latency & streaming UX / next steps

Thanks Marissa - this is great and captures the call. A few clarifications from our side:

- The 600-900ms numbers are for our most common 120-200 token templated responses (customer summaries). Under heavy background batch load (end-of-day reconciliation) we see those numbers degrade to 1-1.5s.
- Streaming issues: startup is usually okay, but mid-stream stalls occur ~5-8% of requests; they manifest as 500-800ms pauses mid-response, which our player currently interprets as a failure.
- Concurrency: our target for GA is to support ~120 concurrent users generating summaries simultaneously (typical burst to 200 during peak). Cost is a constraint - we're trying to keep per-request inference spend under ~$0.003 if possible.

I'll upload a couple of sample traces and one slow-request log to the Drive link you shared and drop the link here once done.

One ask: can Aditya/Ethan propose how Redwood would approach streaming tuning vs batching trade-offs? In particular: how you ensure low startup while still batching for cost efficiency.

Alex
Head of Product, Finly
alex@finly.com

From: Aditya Rao <aditya_rao@redwood.ai>
To: Alex Johnson <alex@finly.com>, Marissa Cole <marissa@redwood.ai>
Cc: Ethan Park <ethan_park@redwood.ai>
Date: Sun, 29 Nov 2026 09:30:00 +0000
Subject: Re: Discovery recap: Finly - p95 latency & streaming UX / next steps

Alex - quick technical note ahead of the deep-dive. High-level approach we'll propose:

1) Measure baseline: token distribution, request size, and KV cache hit rates (we'll need sample traces).
2) Streaming-first policy: prioritize low startup by allocating a small fast-path pool (warm workers) that serve streaming requests with minimal batching; fallback to batched paths for throughput when requests are compatible.
3) Smart batching: use continuous batching with adaptive timeouts to balance startup vs token throughput. We can tune per-route thresholds (e.g., 20ms micro-batch for interactive flows).
4) Prefix/KV caching: pre-warm common prompts, especially for templated summaries, to avoid repeated compute.
5) Canary + metrics: PoC will include p95/p50/p99, time-to-first-byte (TTFB), and stall-rate during streams.

For the PoC we'll want: representative traces, expected qps profile (1-min and 1-hour), and cost target. I'll prepare a short slide with the proposed pool configs + expected latency bands (best effort) ahead of our deep-dive.

- Aditya
Sr. Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference
